You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Comparing the same woman's pink jacket in the source and edited images, is there visible progress toward closing it, even if it is not fully closed?
node.criteria: Pass: visible source-to-edit evidence shows the jacket has moved toward closure, such as reduced separation of the front panels, increased overlap or alignment, or a visible fastening change, while it remains not fully closed. Fail: the relevant front closure is sufficiently visible in both images and shows no change toward closure. Unknown: pose, draping, or occlusion prevents a reliable comparison of those closure cues. Do not treat the jacket merely remaining open as proof of no progress.
node.binding: Compare the same woman and bright pink jacket across source and edited images. Judge closure cues rather than pose or jacket silhouette; account for the changed pose and draping, and use unknown if the corresponding closure region cannot be compared reliably.

node_traces.evidence: The woman’s pose and the jacket’s draping differ substantially between images. The front closure area is not reliably comparable, so visible progress toward closing the jacket cannot be established.

fulfillment: The endpoint check is well grounded: the edited image shows the jacket open, so support 1 should remain a failure. The unresolved result comes from support 2’s comparison, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure. Improve the node’s binding/criteria so progress is judged from the visible jacket closure itself, using the source and edited images while accounting for pose and drape changes; compare whether the front panels or closure have moved toward each other, and return unknown only when that evidence genuinely cannot be assessed. Do not infer progress merely from the jacket’s changed appearance or force the reference label: the images show a substantial pose change and the edited jacket hanging open, so the evidence may still warrant uncertainty about progress.
